title: AI Boom Pushes China's Trade Surplus Past $1 Trillion
paragraphs: China's trade surplus for the first 10 months of 2026 has risen above $1 trillion as investment in AI around the world drives its technology export market.
A trade surplus describes the situation where the value of a country's exports is higher than the value of what it imports from other countries.
In recent months, China — the world's second-largest economy after the US — has seen strong global demand for products used in AI technology, such as computer chips and data center servers.
And China's exports were worth 35% more in October 2026 compared with the same month last year. In September 2026, they were worth 36% more than in September 2025.

If this strong export performance continues, with two more months left in the year, China could be on track for its highest-ever trade surplus. It's already close to the record-breaking $1.2 trillion surplus it achieved across all 12 months of 2025.

There are obvious benefits to trade surpluses — they're good for employment and economic growth, and also strengthen a country's currency. However, this trade surplus doesn't tell China's whole economic story.

China has operated with a trade surplus since the mid-1990s. However, its domestic market is comparatively weak. Chinese consumers save more and spend less money than those in many similarly large economies, saving an average of one-third of what they earn.
Weak domestic demand due to a consumer reluctance to spend means that China relies heavily on the export market, and this leaves it vulnerable to any slowdown in global demand.

Its export boom has also caused issues with trading partners like the US and the EU, which are now trying to limit Chinese products to protect their local businesses. For example, talks between China and the EU last month saw the two parties agree to a limit on exports of Chinese-made hybrid vehicles to Europe.
